claim: Human Cyclin-Dependent-Kinases (CDKs) target the RAD9 subunit of the 9-1-1 checkpoint clamp on Thr292 to modulate DNA damage checkpoint activation.
source: We show that human Cyclin-Dependent-Kinases (CDKs) target the RAD9 subunit of the 9-1-1 checkpoint clamp on Thr292, to modulate DNA damage checkpoint activation.
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assays showing CDK2-CyclinA2 phosphorylates RAD9 at Thr292, and in vivo cell cycle analysis showing phosphorylation at this site.

claim: Thr292 phosphorylation on RAD9 creates a binding site for Polo-Like-Kinase1 (PLK1).
source: Thr292 phosphorylation on RAD9 creates a binding site for Polo-Like-Kinase1 (PLK1), which phosphorylates RAD9 on Thr313.
evidence: Demonstrated by GSH-bead pull-down assays showing PLK1 binds to CDK-phosphorylated RAD9, peptide competition assays, and co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: PLK1 phosphorylates RAD9 on Thr313 after binding to phosphorylated Thr292.
source: Thr292 phosphorylation on RAD9 creates a binding site for Polo-Like-Kinase1 (PLK1), which phosphorylates RAD9 on Thr313.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS analysis identifying pThr313 in PLK1-treated samples and western blotting with phospho-specific antibodies.

claim: CDK-PLK1-dependent phosphorylations of RAD9 suppress checkpoint activation.
source: These CDK-PLK1-dependent phosphorylations of RAD9 suppress checkpoint activation, therefore maintaining high DNA synthesis rates during DNA replication stress.
evidence: Shown by increased CHK1 phosphorylation and chromatin-bound checkpoint proteins in cells expressing phosphorylation-defective RAD9 mutants.

claim: CDK-PLK1-dependent phosphorylations of RAD9 maintain high DNA synthesis rates during DNA replication stress.
source: These CDK-PLK1-dependent phosphorylations of RAD9 suppress checkpoint activation, therefore maintaining high DNA synthesis rates during DNA replication stress.
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU incorporation assays showing reduced DNA synthesis in cells expressing T292A or T313A RAD9 mutants under HU treatment.

claim: The recombinant CDK2-CyclinA2 complex phosphorylates RAD9 at Thr292 in vitro.
source: The recombinant GST-tagged C-terminal (a.a. 266–391) portion of RAD9 was mixed with the purified active CDK2-CyclinA2 complex. Western blotting was performed using the α-RAD9 antibody and the α-pT292 (pT292) and α-phospho-Ser277 (pS277) RAD9 antibodies.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B with western blot detection of pT292 signal after CDK2-CyclinA2 treatment.

claim: The phosphorylation of RAD9 Thr292 is diminished in roscovitine-treated cells.
source: The pThr292 signal was diminished in roscovitine (CDK inhibitor)-treated cells, although the band was still detectable in RO-3306 (CDK1 inhibitor)-treated cells (Meijer et al., 1997; Vassilev et al., 2006).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blotting of cell lysates from cells treated with CDK inhibitors.

claim: Any CDK can phosphorylate Thr292 of RAD9.
source: These results suggested that any CDK would be able to phosphorylate Thr292 of RAD9.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that roscovitine (general CDK inhibitor) but not RO-3306 (CDK1-specific inhibitor) eliminated pThr292 signal.

claim: The phosphorylation of Thr292 was observed weakly from mid S phase and strongly at the G2/M transition.
source: The phosphorylation of Thr292 was observed weakly from mid S phase (6–8 hr in Figure 1C) and strongly at the G2/M transition, a pattern that correlated with the CDK activity.
evidence: Shown by thymidine block-and-release experiments with western blotting at different time points (Figure 1C).

claim: Cells expressing T292A-mutated RAD9 show a slight delay in mitotic commitment.
source: We observed a slight delay in the mitotic commitment, as detected by the delayed appearance of the phosphorylation of histone H3 Ser10, in cells expressing T292A-mutated RAD9 (Figure 1C, bottom).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis showing delayed histone H3 phosphorylation in T292A-expressing cells.

claim: Higher levels of RAD17 and Ser345-phosphorylated CHK1 accumulate in the insoluble fraction of HU-treated cells expressing T292A-mutated RAD9.
source: Indeed, higher levels of RAD17 and the Ser345-phosphorylated CHK1 accumulated in the insoluble fraction of HU-treated cells expressing the T292A-mutated RAD9 (+HU, compare WT and T292A in Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown by chromatin fractionation assay followed by western blotting (Figure 1D).

claim: T292A-mutated RAD9 remains in the insoluble fraction when cells are exposed to HU.
source: In contrast, the T292A-mutated RAD9 (T292A) remained in the insoluble fraction when the cells were exposed to HU.
evidence: Demonstrated by chromatin fractionation assay showing persistent chromatin association of T292A RAD9 under HU treatment.

claim: Cells expressing T292A-mutated RAD9 exhibit an increased population of S-phase cells when treated with 0.2 mM hydroxyurea.
source: However, in presence of 0.2 mM hydroxyurea, although the cells expressing wild-type RAD9 showed similar profiles to the parental U2OS cells, the cells expressing the T292A-mutated RAD9 exhibited an increased population of S-phase cells (Figure 1E, WT: 35.8%, T292A: 43.2%).
evidence: Shown by flow cytometry analysis of DNA content (Figure 1E).

claim: The amount of EdU incorporation in cells expressing T292A-mutated RAD9 was reduced to 60-70% of that in HU-exposed cells expressing wild-type RAD9.
source: However, when these cell lines were treated with 0.2 mM HU for 24 hr, the amount of EdU incorporation in the cells expressing the T292A-mutated RAD9 was reduced to 60–70% of that in the HU-exposed cells expressing wild-type RAD9 (details shown later in Figure 4B, compare WT and T292A).
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU incorporation assay measured by flow cytometry.

claim: The PBD of PLK1 efficiently binds to the C-terminus of RAD9 in a yeast two-hybrid assay.
source: Indeed, we found that the PBD of PLK1, but not those of PLKs2-5, efficiently bound to the C-terminus of RAD9 in a yeast two-hybrid assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown by yeast two-hybrid ONPG assay results.

claim: The binding of PLK1 PBD to RAD9 decreases when Thr292 is substituted with alanine.
source: We further demonstrated that this binding decreased when Thr292 of RAD9 was substituted with alanine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assay comparing wild-type and T292A RAD9.

claim: PLK1 co-precipitates efficiently with GST-RAD9 using GSH-beads only when CDK2-cyclinA2 is present.
source: PLK1 co-precipitated efficiently using GSH-beads, but only when CDK2-cyclinA2 was present (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Shown by in vitro pull-down experiments with GSH-beads.

claim: A bandshift of GST-RAD9 is observed only when PLK1 is present in kinase buffer containing ATP.
source: Notably, this experiment employed a kinase buffer containing ATP, and we observed a bandshift of GST-RAD9 only when PLK1 was present (lane three in Figure 2A, lane one in Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blotting showing mobility shift of GST-RAD9.

claim: PLK1 remains in the supernatant fraction when incubated with a pThr292-containing peptide.
source: PLK1 remained in the supernatant fraction when incubated with a pThr292-containing peptide (pT292), but not when incubated with other peptides (Non-P, pS291, pS291/pT292) or in the absence of a competing peptide (Figure 2C; compare Sup and Beads).
evidence: Shown by peptide competition assay with GSH-bead pull-down.

claim: A pThr292-containing peptide activates PLK1 to phosphorylate RAD9.
source: The bandshift in the anti-RAD9 western blot was only observed in the presence of a pThr292-containing peptide, and the use of other peptides in the reaction did not yield a bandshift (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro kinase assay using GST-RAD9-T292A as substrate with different peptides.

claim: PLK1-HA co-immunoprecipitates with wild-type RAD9-mH but is greatly diminished with T292A-mutated RAD9-mH.
source: The co-IP of PLK1-HA was observed regardless of UV damage stress in cells that expressed wild-type RAD9-mH, and was greatly diminished in cells that expressed the T292A-mutated RAD9-mH (Figure 2E).
evidence: Shown by co-immunoprecipitation experiments using anti-myc antibody.

claim: Endogenous PLK1 co-immunoprecipitates with wild-type RAD9-mH but is decreased with T292A-mutated RAD9-mH.
source: The co-IP of PLK1 was also observed in cells that expressed wild-type RAD9-mH, but was decreased in cells that expressed the T292A-mutated RAD9-mH (Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation of endogenous PLK1.

claim: Significant amounts of pThr313 and pSer326 were detected in GST-RAD9 when incubated with both CDK2-CycA2 and PLK1.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, significant amounts of pThr313 and pSer326 were detected in GST-RAD9, when it was incubated with both CDK2-CycA2 and PLK1.
evidence: Demonstrated by LC-MS/MS analysis of phosphorylated GST-RAD9.

claim: Thr313 and Ser326 of RAD9 are followed by hydrophobic amino acids and match the PLK1 phosphorylation consensus sequence.
source: Furthermore, the Thr313 and Ser326 residues of RAD9 are followed by hydrophobic amino acids, and thus Thr313 and Ser326 match the previously reported PLK1 phosphorylation consensus sequence (Nakajima et al., 2003).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and comparison to known PLK1 consensus sequences from literature.

claim: RAD9 Thr313 and Ser326 constitute sites that are phosphorylated by PLK1.
source: These results indicated that RAD9 Thr313 and Ser326 constitute sites that are phosphorylated by PLK1.
evidence: Concluded from LC-MS/MS data and consensus sequence analysis.

claim: The region around the Thr313 phosphorylation site is conserved among vertebrate RAD9A proteins.
source: The region around the Thr313 phosphorylation site is conserved among the vertebrate RAD9A proteins (In this manuscript, RAD9 is used synonymously with RAD9A unless otherwise stated.) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown by sequence alignment of RAD9A proteins from multiple vertebrate species.

claim: RAD9B proteins lack the PLK1 phosphorylation sites identified in RAD9A.
source: Interestingly, the RAD9B proteins, which are paralogues that are thought to function in testis and/or to have distinct functions (Dufault et al., 2003; Leloup et al., 2010; Pérez-Castro and Freire, 2012), lack the PLK1 phosphorylation sites identified here (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by sequence comparison between RAD9A and RAD9B, with reference to literature on RAD9B function.

claim: The appearance of both pThr313 and pSer326 signals depends on the presence of CDK2-cyclinA2.
source: As demonstrated by western blotting, the appearance of both the pThr313 and pSer326 signals depended on the presence of CDK2-cyclinA2 (Figure 3C, quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Shown by in vitro kinase assays with and without CDK2-cyclinA2 pretreatment.

claim: Large decreases in pThr313 and pSer326 western blot signals were observed when GST-RAD9-T292A was used as substrate in the PLK1 kinase assay.
source: Furthermore, large decreases in the pThr313 and pSer326 western blot signals were observed when GST-RAD9-T292A was used as the substrate in the PLK1 kinase assay (Figure 3D, quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro kinase assays comparing wild-type and T292A RAD9.

claim: PLK1 mediates the phosphorylation of Thr313 of RAD9 in cells.
source: When the western blot was probed using the antibody against pThr313, the signals were seen with the expression of PLK1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, lane 2). These signals completely disappeared when the PLK1-KR mutant was expressed and the cells were treated with the PLK1 inhibitor BI2536 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, lane 3). Together, these results suggested that PLK1 mediates the phosphorylation of Thr313 of RAD9.
evidence: Shown by immunoprecipitation and western blotting in cells expressing PLK1 or kinase-dead PLK1 with PLK1 inhibitor treatment.

claim: Ser326 can be phosphorylated by kinases other than PLK1.
source: When the blots were instead probed with the antibody against pSer326, again the signals were detected when PLK1 was expressed, but these signals were decreased only slightly when PLK1-KR was expressed and the cells were treated with BI2536 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, compare lanes 2 and 3). This suggested that Ser326 can be phosphorylated by kinases other than PLK1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pSer326 signal persists even when PLK1 is inhibited.

claim: The pThr292 signal increased in BI2536-treated cells.
source: However, the pThr292 signal, which was relatively unchanged in the UV-irradiated cells, was increased in the BI2536-treated cells (Figure 3E, IP; lanes 5 and 6), implying that this CDK-dependent phosphorylation event (pThr292) occurred upstream of the PLK1-dependent phosphorylation.
evidence: Shown by immunoprecipitation and western blotting of RAD9 from cells treated with PLK1 inhibitor.

claim: Diminished pThr313 levels were observed when cells were treated with BI2536 or when T292A-mutated RAD9 was expressed.
source: We observed diminished pThr313 levels when the cells were treated with BI2536 (Figure 3E, lanes 5 and 6), or when T292A-mutated RAD9 was expressed (Figure 3E, lanes 7, 8 and 9) instead of wild-type RAD9 (WT).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and western blotting under different conditions.

claim: The pThr313 signal increased slightly when cells were UV-irradiated.
source: Interestingly, the pThr313 signal increased slightly when the cells were UV-irradiated (Figure 3E, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: Shown by immunoprecipitation and western blotting of UV-treated cells.

claim: The pSer326 signal increased upon UV irradiation and showed a slight decrease when cells were treated with BI2536.
source: We also observed that the pSer326 signal increased upon UV irradiation, and a slight decrease was detected when the cells were treated with BI2536 (Figure 3E, lanes 5 and 6).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and western blotting.

claim: No decrease of pSer326 was observed in T292A-mutated RAD9.
source: However, we did not see a decrease of pSer326 in the T292A-mutated RAD9 (Figure 3E, lanes 7, 8 and 9).
evidence: Shown by immunoprecipitation and western blotting of cells expressing T292A RAD9.

claim: The amount of pThr292 was somewhat decreased by HU exposure in synchronized cells.
source: Although the total amounts of (RAD9), pThr313 (pT313), and pSer 326 (pS326) were relatively unchanged by the HU exposure, the amount of pThr292 (pT292) was somewhat decreased.
evidence: Shown by immunoprecipitation analysis of synchronized cells treated with HU.

claim: Increased accumulation of T313A-mutated RAD9 in the insoluble fraction was observed upon HU treatment.
source: In a fractionation assay, we observed the increased accumulation of T313A-mutated RAD9 in the insoluble fraction upon HU treatment (Figure 4A, Triton-X insoluble, +HU).
evidence: Demonstrated by chromatin fractionation assay followed by western blotting.

claim: Accumulation of Ser345-phosphorylated CHK1 in the insoluble fraction was observed in HU-treated cells expressing T313A-mutated RAD9.
source: We also observed the accumulation of Ser345-phosphorylated CHK1 in the insoluble fraction of HU-treated cells that expressed the T313A-mutated RAD9 (Figure 4A, Triton-X insoluble, +HU).
evidence: Shown by chromatin fractionation assay and western blotting.

claim: Lower levels of S326A-mutated RAD9 accumulated in the insoluble fraction compared to T313A-mutated RAD9.
source: It should be noted that lower levels of the S326A-mutated RAD9 accumulated in the insoluble fraction (compared to the accumulation of RAD9-T313A under the same conditions).
evidence: Observed in chromatin fractionation assay comparing different RAD9 mutants.

claim: The inhibition of PLK1 activity by BI2536 causes accumulation of endogenous RAD9 in the insoluble fraction when cells are treated with HU.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, we also observed that the inhibition of the PLK1 activity by BI2536 also caused the accumulation of endogenous RAD9 in the insoluble fraction, when the cells were treated with HU (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by chromatin fractionation assay of cells treated with PLK1 inhibitor and HU.

claim: TopBP1 and CLASPIN accumulated in the insoluble fraction upon inhibition of PLK1 in HU-treated cells.
source: Since both TopBP1 and CLASPIN, which act as mediators for checkpoint signaling, also accumulated in the insoluble fraction upon the inhibition of PLK1 in HU-treated cells, we concluded that a PLK1-dependent phosphorylation event controls the association of the checkpoint machinery with chromatin.
evidence: Shown by chromatin fractionation assay with PLK1 inhibitor treatment.

claim: Cells expressing T313A-mutated RAD9 showed a significantly lower level of EdU incorporation compared to cells expressing wild-type RAD9 under HU treatment.
source: The cells that expressed the T313A-mutated RAD9 showed a significantly lower level of EdU incorporation, as compared to the cells that expressed wild-type RAD9 (as seen in T292A-RAD9 expressing cells) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU incorporation assay measured by flow cytometry.

claim: Cells expressing S326A-mutated RAD9 and those expressing wild-type RAD9 incorporated similar levels of EdU.
source: The cells that expressed the S326A-mutated RAD9 and those expressing wild-type RAD9 incorporated similar levels of EdU.
evidence: Shown by EdU incorporation assay comparing different RAD9 mutants.

claim: The transfection of siRAD9 in cells expressing T313A-mutated RAD9 yielded an enhancement in the phosphorylation of Ser345 of CHK1.
source: In cells that expressed the T313A-mutated RAD9, the transfection of siRAD9 yielded an enhancement in the phosphorylation of Ser345 of CHK1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B) and a slight reduction in the rate of DNA replication upon HU treatment, as compared to cells that were not treated with siRAD9 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blotting and EdU incorporation assay in siRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: The reduction in DNA replication rate was confirmed in telomerase-positive HEK293A cells expressing T292A- or T313A-mutated RAD9.
source: Furthermore, we also confirmed the reduction in the DNA replication rate in telomerase-positive HEK293A cells (Bryan et al., 1995) expressing either T292A- or T313A-mutated RAD9 (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: Shown by EdU incorporation assay in HEK293A cells.

claim: Aphidicolin treatment reduced the rate of EdU incorporation in cells expressing T313A-mutated RAD9.
source: Specifically, aphidicolin treatment also reduced the rate of EdU incorporation, and MMC treatment caused more cells to accumulate in early S phase when the T313A-mutated RAD9 was expressed, although the latter treatment did not yield an obvious decrease in the EdU incorporation (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU incorporation assay under different genotoxic stress conditions.

claim: The rates of individual replication forks in cells expressing RAD9-WT were 0.85 ± 0.36 kb/minutes in the absence of HU.
source: In the absence of HU, the rates of individual replication forks in cells that expressed RAD9-WT were 0.85 ± 0.36 kb/minutes, and those of the RAD9-T313A expressing cells were slower (0.66 ± 0.27 kb/minutes, p-value: 5.8 × 10−7).
evidence: Measured by DNA combing assay.

claim: The rates of individual replication forks in cells expressing RAD9-T313A were 0.66 ± 0.27 kb/minutes in the absence of HU.
source: In the absence of HU, the rates of individual replication forks in cells that expressed RAD9-WT were 0.85 ± 0.36 kb/minutes, and those of the RAD9-T313A expressing cells were slower (0.66 ± 0.27 kb/minutes, p-value: 5.8 × 10−7).
evidence: Measured by DNA combing assay.

claim: The IOD values were 131 ± 62 kb in RAD9-WT expressing cells and 107 ± 61 kb in RAD9-T313A expressing cells in the absence of HU.
source: The IOD values were 131 ± 62 kb in RAD9-WT expressing cells, and 107 ± 61 kb in RAD9-T313A expressing cells.
evidence: Measured by DNA combing assay.

claim: Under HU stress, the rates of DNA replication forks became slower in both RAD9-WT and RAD9-T313A expressing cells with similar velocities.
source: We then measured the fork rates under the HU stress, and observed that the rates of the DNA replication forks became slower in both RAD9-WT and RAD9-T313A expressing cells, with similar velocities (WT: 0.37 ± 0.16 kb/minutes, T313A: 0.37 ± 0.19 kb/minutes).
evidence: Measured by DNA combing assay under HU treatment.

claim: Under HU conditions, the IOD of RAD9-T313A expressing cells was slightly longer than that of RAD9-WT expressing cells.
source: Under these conditions, the IOD of the RAD9-T313A expressing cells was slightly longer than that of RAD9-WT expressing cells (WT: 61 ± 38 kb, T313A: 69 ± 41 kb), although the difference is marginally significant (p-value: 0.058).
evidence: Measured by DNA combing assay under HU treatment.

claim: T292A- or T313A-mutated RAD9 co-immunoprecipitated with increased amounts of CLASPIN upon HU treatment.
source: Finally, we observed that the T292A- or T313A-mutated RAD9 co-immunoprecipitated with increased amounts of CLASPIN upon HU treatment ((Figure 5—figure supplement 2), see 'HU' in IP).
evidence: Shown by co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Cells expressing T292A- or T313A-mutated RAD9 exhibited a slower growth rate in the presence of HU.
source: Indeed, we observed that cells expressing the T292A- or T313A-mutated RAD9 exhibited a slower growth rate in the presence of HU (For U2OS cells, Figure 6A; for HEK293A cells, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by cell growth assays using Presto-Blue reagent.

claim: Cells expressing T313A-mutated RAD9 exhibited a significant decrease in colony-forming efficiency upon exposure to 0.2 mM HU.
source: Additionally, as compared to the cells that expressed wild-type RAD9, the cells that expressed T313A-mutated RAD9 exhibited a significant decrease in colony-forming efficiency (as assessed by a cell viability assay) upon exposure to 0.2 mM HU (Figure 6B).
evidence: Shown by colony formation assay.

claim: The DNA damage checkpoint delays cell cycle progression when cells are exposed to genotoxic stress.
source: Genomic DNA damage is a type of environmental stress, and when cells are exposed to genotoxic stress, cell cycle progression is delayed by a mechanism called the DNA damage checkpoint.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of cell cycle and DNA damage response.

claim: The delay in cell cycle progression increases the time available for DNA repair processes.
source: Although the delay increases the time available for DNA repair processes to perform damage recovery (Elledge, 1996; Weinert and Hartwell, 1988), the degree of the checkpoint response must be tightly regulated, depending on the proliferative status of the cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to foundational work on DNA damage checkpoints.

claim: CDKs are the primary driving forces that order and coordinate cell cycle events.
source: Among the pro-mitotic activities, CDKs are the primary driving forces that order and coordinate cell cycle events (Swaffer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on CDK function.

claim: Activation by CDKs controls temporally ordered programs throughout the cell cycle, such as replication origin firing.
source: Activation by CDKs not only initiates M-phase events, but also controls temporally ordered programs throughout the cell cycle, such as replication origin firing upon initiation of DNA replication, which potentially support proliferation (Stern and Nurse, 1996; Tanaka et al., 2007; Trovesi et al., 2013; Zegerman and Diffley, 2007).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on CDK-dependent cell cycle control.

claim: Stalled replication forks expose single-stranded DNA, which is recognized by checkpoint signaling complexes that activate the S-phase checkpoint.
source: The stalled replication forks expose single-stranded DNA, which is recognized by checkpoint signaling complexes that activate the S-phase checkpoint (Giannattasio and Branzei, 2017; Katou et al., 2003; Sogo et al., 2002; Zou and Elledge, 2003; Zou et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on S-phase checkpoint activation.

claim: Checkpoint signaling reduces the rate of S-phase progression by repressing late origin firing or by slowing the progression of individual replication forks.
source: When the DNA damage response is dominant, checkpoint signaling reduces the rate of S-phase progression by repressing late origin firing or by slowing the progression of individual replication forks.
evidence: This is established knowledge about checkpoint function in S-phase.

claim: PLK1 is the key protein involved in pro-mitotic activity to override DNA damage checkpoint signaling.
source: The key protein involved in the pro-mitotic activity to override DNA damage checkpoint signaling is PLK1.
evidence: Inferred from the discussion of PLK1's role in checkpoint adaptation and override.

claim: Adaptation was initially reported in budding yeast where cells override a G2 DNA damage checkpoint via a CDC5-dependent mechanism.
source: This phenomenon was initially reported as adaptation, and was originally described in a budding yeast system in which cells overrode a G2 DNA damage checkpoint via a CDC5 (budding yeast PLK1 orthologue)-dependent mechanism, after prolonged G2 arrest induced by irreparable DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) (Pellicioli et al., 2001; Sandell and Zakian, 1993; Toczyski et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to original work on checkpoint adaptation in yeast.

claim: Adaptation was reported in Xenopus where a prolonged aphidicolin-induced replication block was compromised by a Plx1-dependent process.
source: Adaptation was also reported in a Xenopus system, in which a prolonged aphidicolin-induced replication block was compromised by a Plx1 (Xenopus PLK1 orthologue)-dependent process (Yoo et al., 2004), and an analogous phenomenon has also been reported in mammalian cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to work on checkpoint adaptation in Xenopus.

claim: Mammalian cells only activate the G2/M DNA damage checkpoint when a certain amount of DNA damage is present.
source: However, mammalian cells only activate the G2/M DNA damage checkpoint when a certain amount of DNA damage (e.g. ~20 DSBs) is present.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian checkpoint thresholds.

claim: Mammalian cells can enter mitosis even in the presence of DNA damage signals such as γ-H2AX foci.
source: Indeed, mammalian cells can enter mitosis even in the presence of DNA damage signals, such as γ-H2AX foci (Deckbar et al., 2007; Ishikawa et al., 2010; Syljuåsen et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on mammalian cell checkpoint behavior.

claim: When cellular PLK1 activity reaches a certain level, cells can re-enter mitosis upon recovery from G2 checkpoint arrest.
source: When the cellular PLK1 activity reaches a certain level, the cells can re-enter mitosis upon recovery from G2 checkpoint arrest (Liang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to work on PLK1 and mitotic entry.

claim: PLK1 functions during S phase or a related DNA damage response, facilitating DNA metabolism in support of rapid cell proliferation.
source: In fact, PLK1 functions not only upon mitotic commitment, but also during S phase or a related DNA damage response, thereby facilitating DNA metabolism in support of rapid cell proliferation (Moudry et al., 2016; Yata et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on PLK1 function in S phase.

claim: The PLK1 protein contains a Polo-Box Domain (PBD) that recognizes a pre-phosphorylated substrate.
source: Importantly, the PLK1 protein contains a Polo-Box Domain (PBD) that recognizes a pre-phosphorylated substrate (Elia et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to work characterizing PLK1 PBD function.

claim: The PBD preferentially recognizes phospho-serine/threonine (-S-pS/pT-P-)-containing peptides.
source: The substrate is phosphorylated by a kinase, typically a CDK, and the PBD preferentially recognizes phospho-serine/threonine (-S-pS/pT-P-)-containing peptides (van Vugt et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to work on PBD substrate specificity.

claim: The 9-1-1 complex acts as a DNA damage sensor protein complex in checkpoint signaling.
source: We found that CDK targeted RAD9, a subunit of the DNA clamp complex 9-1-1, which acts as a DNA damage sensor protein complex in checkpoint signaling (Delacroix et al., 2007; Furuya et al., 2004; Kumagai et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2012; Navadgi-Patil and Burgers, 2009; St Onge et al., 2003; Takeishi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on 9-1-1 complex function.

claim: The CDK-dependent phosphorylation of RAD9 at residue 292 was originally identified by Davey's group.
source: The phosphorylation of RAD9 Thr292 was originally identified by Davey's group (St Onge et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to original work identifying this phosphorylation site.

claim: The interaction between a PBD and phospho-peptide is strong, with a dissociation constant in the range of a few hundred nanomolar.
source: The interaction between a PBD and the phospho-peptide is reportedly strong, with a dissociation constant in the range of a few hundred nanomolar (van Vugt et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to work characterizing PBD-peptide binding affinity.

claim: PBD can act as an auto-inhibitor of the PLK1 kinase domain, and binding of a substrate to the PBD counteracts this auto-inhibitory function.
source: The PBD can reportedly act as an auto-inhibitor of the PLK1 kinase domain, and the binding of a substrate to the PBD counteracts this auto-inhibitory function (Jang et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to work on PLK1 auto-inhibition mechanism.

claim: RAD9's function as a DNA damage sensor is the target of PLK1-dependent regulation.
source: We speculate that RAD9's function as a DNA damage sensor is the target of PLK1-dependent regulation, given that we observed increased amounts of RAD9 on the chromatin when PLK1 failed to phosphorylate RAD9.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed data showing increased chromatin-bound RAD9 in phosphorylation-defective mutants.

claim: The PLK1-dependent phosphorylation of RAD9 would minimize the amount of RAD9 bound at sites of stalled replication forks or replicative DNA damage.
source: The PLK1-dependent phosphorylation of RAD9 would minimize the amount of RAD9 bound at sites of stalled replication forks or replicative DNA damage, possibly by giving dynamism to the 9-1-1 complex from the DNA ends, and may in turn reduce the number of active checkpoint complexes.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the observed increased chromatin association of phosphorylation-defective RAD9.

claim: The region phosphorylated by PLK1 is close to the region required for association with the single-stranded-DNA binding protein RP-A.
source: For example, the region phosphorylated by PLK1 is close to the region required for the association with the single-stranded-DNA binding protein RP-A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)(Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and citation to work on RAD9-RPA interaction.

claim: The rate of S-phase progression is related to the number of available replication origins in eukaryotic cells.
source: In eukaryotic cells, the rate of S-phase progression is related to the number of available replication origins (Yekezare et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on replication origin control.

claim: S-phase checkpoint signaling inhibits the firing of late-replication origins when the signaling is dominant.
source: Upon growth under genotoxic stress, the replication rate can be controlled by S-phase checkpoint signaling, and when the signaling is dominant, it inhibits the firing of the late-replication origins (Santocanale and Diffley, 1998; Shirahige et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to work on checkpoint control of origin firing.

claim: The inhibition of origin firing might prevent the generation of additional replicative stress in un-replicated regions of the genome.
source: This inhibition of origin firing might prevent the generation of additional replicative stress in un-replicated regions of the genome, and would suppress genomic instability (Boos et al., 2011; Petermann et al., 2010; Yekezare et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on replication stress and genomic instability.

claim: The slow S phase progression rate could be caused by reduction in the progression rate of individual replication forks, which is dependent on CHK1 activation.
source: Alternatively, the slow S phase progression rate could be caused by the reduction in the progression rate of individual replication forks, which is reportedly dependent on CHK1 activation upon camptothecin-induced stress, and may allow the fork to mount a more robust response to the damage (Iyer and Rhind, 2013; Seiler et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to work on CHK1-dependent fork slowing.

claim: The reduction of fork speed results in activation of dormant origins proximal to the stalled replication fork, which may compensate for decreases in local DNA replication rate.
source: It has also been proposed that the reduction of the fork speed results in the activation of dormant origins proximal to the stalled replication fork, a process that may compensate for decreases in the local rate of DNA replication (Yekezare et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to work on dormant origin activation.

claim: The slower S-phase progression in T313A-RAD9 expressing cells is not caused by slower velocity of DNA replication forks.
source: The DNA fiber/combing assay under the HU treated conditions revealed that the velocities of the replication forks were the same between the WT- and T313A-RAD9 expressing cells. This could indicate that the slower S-phase progression seen in the T313A-mutated cells was not caused by the slower velocity of the DNA replication forks.
evidence: Demonstrated by DNA combing assay showing similar fork velocities under HU treatment.

claim: A moderate activation of the S-phase checkpoint exists even in the normal cell cycle process in T313A-RAD9 expressing U2OS cells.
source: Perhaps more significantly, even under non-stressed conditions, we observed a slower DNA replication fork velocity in the T313A-RAD9 expressing cells, as compared to that in WT-RAD9 expressing cells. This could indicate that a moderate activation of the S-phase checkpoint exists even in the normal cell cycle process in the T313A-RAD9 expressing U2OS cells.
evidence: Inferred from DNA combing data showing slower fork velocity in non-stressed T313A cells.

claim: PLK1 may raise the threshold of DNA damage level required for checkpoint activation during S-phase.
source: In the T313A-expressing cells, further exposure to HU-induced stress would activate an excessive DNA damage response and could cause a reduction in the number of firing origins, which would result in a slower rate of S-phase progression. In this scenario, PLK1 may raise the threshold of the DNA damage level, which would require more DNA damage stress for the checkpoint activation during S-phase.
evidence: This is a speculative model to explain the observed phenotypes.

claim: The PLK1-dependent phosphorylation of RAD9 may suppress the activation step of the checkpoint rather than diminishing activated DNA damage checkpoint processes.
source: In other words, the PLK1-dependent phosphorylation of RAD9 may suppress the activation step of the checkpoint, rather than diminishing the activated DNA damage checkpoint processes, and this process could act as a novel DNA damage tolerance mechanism to facilitate cell proliferation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism based on the observed data.

claim: PLK1 promotes DNA replication by phosphorylating Orc2, which may be critical to maintain genomic DNA replication under replicative stress.
source: In addition to its role in antagonizing the DNA damage checkpoint activity, PLK1 reportedly promotes DNA replication by phosphorylating Orc2, an event that may be critical to maintain genomic DNA replication under replicative stress (Song et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to work on PLK1 phosphorylation of Orc2.

claim: The PLK1-mediated phosphorylation of Ser188 of Orc2 is responsible for resistance of pancreatic tumor cells to gemcitabine.
source: The PLK1-mediated phosphorylation of Ser188 of Orc2 is responsible for the resistance of pancreatic tumor cells to the chemotherapy drug gemcitabine, an agent that inhibits DNA replication (Song et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to work on Orc2 phosphorylation and drug resistance.

claim: PLK1 employs multiple targets to drive S-phase progression in cells under stress, facilitating tolerance to genotoxic stresses.
source: Combined with our finding of the PLK1-dependent phosphorylation of RAD9, these results suggest that PLK1 employs multiple targets to drive S-phase progression in cells under stress, thus facilitating tolerance to genotoxic stresses.
evidence: This is an inference combining the current findings with previous literature on PLK1 function.

claim: The ectopic expression of PLK1 is associated with a wide range of tumor types.
source: Indeed, the ectopic expression of PLK1 is associated with a wide range of tumor types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PLK1 expression in cancer.

claim: PLK1 is involved in promoting resistance to chemotherapeutic regimens with drugs such as doxorubicin or gemcitabine.
source: PLK1 is also known to be involved in promoting resistance to chemotherapeutic regimens with drugs such as doxorubicin (a DNA intercalating compound) or gemcitabine (a DNA analogue that serves as an inhibitor of DNA replication) (Gutteridge et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to work on PLK1 and chemotherapy resistance.

claim: CDK and PLK1 target the DNA damage sensor RAD9 to minimize the checkpoint response.
source: In summary, we demonstrated that CDK and PLK1 target the DNA damage sensor RAD9 to minimize the checkpoint response, and revealed an underlying mechanism whereby cells can tolerate genotoxic stress and proceed with proliferation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by all the experimental data presented.

claim: A complex balancing mechanism exists to coordinate proliferation and the stress response.
source: Thus, a complex balancing mechanism exists to coordinate proliferation and the stress response, and more systematic investigations of this mechanism should be conducted in the future.
evidence: This is a concluding statement that synthesizes the findings and suggests future directions.

claim: The CDK-PLK1 axis targets RAD9 to antagonize the ability of the DNA damage checkpoint to detect DNA damage.
source: Our results suggest that CDK locally initiates a PLK1-dependent signaling response that antagonizes the ability of the DNA damage checkpoint to detect DNA damage.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings showing that phosphorylation-defective RAD9 mutants have enhanced checkpoint activation and chromatin association.

claim: The CDK-PLK1-dependent control of DNA damage detection by RAD9 plays a crucial role in minimizing DNA damage checkpoint response to promote cell proliferation under genotoxic stress.
source: These results implied that the CDK-/PLK1-dependent control of DNA damage detection by RAD9 plays a crucial role in minimizing the DNA damage checkpoint response, thus helping to drive proliferation under conditions of DNA replicative stress.
evidence: This is a concluding interpretation based on all the experimental evidence showing effects on checkpoint activation, DNA synthesis rates, and cell growth.
